speaker: Doctor
text: Let's start by asking: How long have you noticed this breast mass, and has its size or shape changed over time? Are you experiencing any pain, nipple discharge, or skin changes like dimpling or redness in the affected area?

speaker: Patient
text: 48-year-old woman. The patient noticed a mass in her left breast 4 weeks ago, which has rapidly increased in size. She denies any recent trauma or infections. No history of similar complaints in the past.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that history. To further evaluate the rapid growth and age of onset, have you noticed any changes in your menstrual cycle or any family history of breast cancer? REQUEST TEST: Mammography, Bilateral Ultrasound.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is concerning; a rapidly growing mass with normal imaging findings suggests the lesion may be too small for mammography or ultrasound to detect, or it may be located in an area difficult to visualize. Have you noticed any nipple retraction, inversion, or discharge from the affected breast? REQUEST TEST: Breast MRI with contrast.

speaker: Doctor
text: This is highly unusual; both mammography and MRI are negative despite your report of a rapidly growing mass. Have you experienced any fever, chills, or recent skin infections in the area? REQUEST TEST: Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) and request clinical images of the mass.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) results are inconclusive due to insufficient sample; clinical images submitted show a 6-cm, nontender, multinodular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with smooth polylobulated contours and no associated skin changes or lymphadenopathy.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Fibroadenomatosis (multiple fibroadenomas). While the rapid growth is atypical for simple fibroadenomas and warrants long-term monitoring, the imaging characteristics of a smooth, polylobulated, nontender mass in a 48-year-old are most consistent with benign proliferative breast disease rather than malignancy. I recommend serial ultrasounds every 6 months to monitor for changes in size or morphology.
